newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Economists predict cautious UK budget.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Economists predict cautious UK budget.

text.p: The British government is expected to give away a net 2.25 billion sterling in tax cuts in next Tuesday's budget, but the overall impact of the financial package will be neutral to cautious, a Reuters survey showed on Thursday.

The survey, which canvassed opinions of 27 London-based economists between November 18 and 19, showed Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke would trim one penny off the basic rate of income tax, down to 23 pence from 24 pence, but would claw back the cost by cutting spending, economists said.
"The tax cuts, at most, are the icing on the cake, but it's a pretty thin layer of icing," said Simon Briscoe, Nikko Europe's UK economist.
The survey findings reflect a view which is already being widely predicted by British commentators and most analysts.

"I expect a relatively tight budget," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International. "The chancellor should unveil modest tax cuts and a rise in thresholds and higher personal allowances, financed by spending cuts."
Indirect taxes should provide some extra source of income for the government, with at least inflation-linked hikes on the standard targets of tobacco, alcohol and petrol excise duties.

"Clarke will have to look at other areas to increase taxation to be able to pay for income tax -- perhaps some larger-than-expected hikes in duties on tobacco and petrol, and perhaps some savings on PRP," said Union Discount's chief economist, Philip Shaw.
Employees receive tax relief on profit-related pay (PRP), which can save them paying tax on up to 4,000 sterling of their salary.
Economists stressed that the value of the tax cuts, in terms of feeding through to the rest of the economy, should not be exaggerated.
"This is more an issue of efficiency than macro-economic management. It's all about incentives and not manipulating or boosting the economy," said Steve Hannah at IBJ International.

Respondents were divided on whether the tax cuts could be deemed as prudent in a healthy economy buoyed by consumer demand. Some saw Clarke being under political pressure to line the pockets of the electorate in his last budget before a general election, which must be held by next May.
"Were we not due to have a general election in the near future, then the issue of tax cuts might be off the agenda for a while," said Union Discount's Shaw.
But others disagreed, saying there were sound economic reasons for the cuts.
"I think the political judgement is supported by the economic environment so I dont see it as being tax cuts motivated by politics," said Briscoe.
And as the overall measures were likely to reduce government borrowing, known as the public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR), markets look set to take Tuesday's measures in their stride.
"So as long as the budget isn't a revenue giveaway then the markets won't be particularly perturbed," said Trevor Williams, economic adviser at Lloyds TSB.
Economists reckon Clarke will reduce his PSBR forecasts to 26 billion sterling from 27 billion for 1996/97, and to 21 billion from 23 billion in 1997/98.
To offset the tax giveaway, Clarke is likely to make some modest cuts in spending, economists said.

One likely move would be to chop in half the contingency reserve, a "rainy day" fund for unexpected developments, which would save 2.5 billion sterling. Clarke would also be expected to keep a tight hold on departmental purse strings.

"He can get three billion by tightening spending in some departments, particularly in social security," said Williams, adding that social security spending was falling anyway because of the upswing in the British economy.
The survey predicted the government would increase its inflation target to 2.5 percent from 2.25 percent in the fourth quarter of 1997.
But this was acceptable in the current strong economic environment, and was still well within the 1-4 percent target range, economists said.
Growth forecasts of 2.5 percent for 1996 and 3.25 percent for 1997 look set to remain unchanged.
Not one of the economists surveyed expected a change in interest rates before or during the budget.
